name: AI and Authorship
title: AI and Authorship
answer: AI and authorship covers who, or what, can be credited with creating a text, an image, a dataset or a piece of code, and how that credit is recorded, transferred and defended. It sits inside governance, ethics and research integrity because authorship is the point where creative or scholarly work meets accountability: a named author is the person a reader, an editor, a funder or a court can hold to what was produced. The topic spans academic publishing, journalism, software, music and visual art, and it also reaches into the machinery of research itself, where model-generated text may appear in a draft, a review or a grant application. The central question is not whether machines can produce plausible output, but what claims of human responsibility survive when they do.

sections.body: AI and authorship covers who, or what, can be credited with creating a text, an image, a dataset or a piece of code, and how that credit is recorded, transferred and defended. sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The practical infrastructure is a mix of disclosure forms, contributor statements, version histories and licence records. Journals and conferences rely on authorship criteria such as those from the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors, which tie credit to substantial contribution, drafting or critical revision, final approval and accountability for the whole work. Publishers, funders and institutions increasingly ask for a statement describing any use of generative tools, and preprint servers, repositories and submission systems carry metadata fields for that purpose. Underneath sit the ordinary tools of scholarly record keeping: DOIs, ORCID identifiers, copyright transfer agreements, and the revision histories that show who changed what and when.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: In practice, people handle AI and authorship by separating assistance from attribution. A writer may use a language model to outline, translate, summarise literature or check grammar, then disclose that use in a methods or acknowledgements section rather than listing the model as an author, since a model cannot consent, hold copyright or answer for errors. Research integrity offices and journal editors typically ask for the prompts or the extent of use, the human who reviewed and verified the output, and a judgement about whether the contribution was substantive. Where a model's output is woven into a paper, the human author remains responsible for accuracy, citations and originality, and plagiarism checks still apply. The working test is simple: if a person cannot be asked to defend a sentence, that person cannot be its author.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The rules here come from several directions at once. Copyright offices and courts in different countries have reached different conclusions about whether machine-generated material can be protected, and registration guidance has shifted as a result. Publishers set their own policies on disclosure and on whether AI tools may be listed as authors, and most major ones say they may not. Research funders and universities add integrity codes, misconduct procedures and training requirements, while data protection law can constrain what gets fed into a third-party model in the first place. Provenance matters throughout: a clear record of which model, which version, which prompts and which human edits supports both credit and correction if something turns out to be wrong, fabricated or copied.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward finer-grained credit rather than a single byline. Contributor role taxonomies, model cards, dataset documentation and provenance standards are being adapted to record assisted work, and some publishers are experimenting with statements that describe the division of labour between person and tool. Detection remains unreliable, so the emphasis is shifting from catching use to requiring disclosure and verifiable process. Expect continuing divergence between jurisdictions on ownership, more explicit journal and funder policies, and growing pressure to treat the human who signs off as the accountable author regardless of how much text a model produced. The unresolved questions are about training data, consent and compensation, and those will keep authorship arguments alive well beyond the byline.
